case_study_insert.main_stem: Suncourt Logistics (SCL) is a cooperative in the regional logistics and distribution sector, delivering groceries and consumer goods from two solar-powered distribution hubs. Founded in 1998 by Carla Jensen, it employs a workforce of 85 and operates a hierarchical structure with democratic leadership and an elected member board. SCL plans to invest $950,000 in a third rooftop solar array and 40 electric last-mile delivery vans, financed by a $600,000 bank loan and $350,000 retained profit. It has fixed costs of $510,000 a year, a variable cost of $30 a unit and a selling price of $46, and currently produces 48,000 units a year. SCL faces one operational problem: absenteeism among warehouse operatives and drivers has reached 10%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Operations Log — Q3 2026: SCL's rooftop solar arrays generated 1.9 GWh in the quarter, covering 71% of warehouse electricity demand, up from 58% a year earlier. Electric vans completed 18,400 last-mile deliveries at a 95.1% on-time rate; customer complaints fell from 31 to 19 per month. Market research of 700 retail customers found that 62% prefer a cooperative supplier with renewable energy and 49% would accept slightly slower delivery windows for lower-carbon drops. A training needs analysis shows 14 of 85 staff have not completed forklift and solar-roof safety training; courses at the regional skills centre cost $600 per employee. A training needs analysis found that drivers need on-the-job training on van routing and off-the-job training in safety standards; members also support a profit sharing scheme for last-mile teams.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Suncourt Logistics for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Business Bulletin (November 2026): (1) Commercial electricity prices have risen 17.5% year-on-year, increasing costs for grid-powered warehouses. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.1% from $12.75 to $13.53 per hour from April 2027, raising wage bills across distribution and haulage. (3) The central bank has raised the base interest rate from 4.5% to 5.25%, increasing borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans.

questions.question_text: SCL plans to fund the third rooftop solar array and 40 electric vans with a $600,000 bank loan. Explain two advantages for SCL of using the bank loan rather than raising additional member share capital.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: A $600,000 bank loan leaves the elected member board and founding members controlling SCL's one-member-one-vote structure unchanged, whereas raising member share capital would dilute existing members' stakes and raise expectations of higher surplus distributions. For a democratic cooperative whose selling point is member ownership, preserving that control protects the values that win contracts from the 62% of 700 surveyed retail customers who prefer a cooperative supplier with renewable energy.

Point 2: Loan repayments are scheduled and predictable, letting SCL match them against the cash savings the new rooftop array generates — already covering 71% of warehouse electricity demand and rising — while keeping its $350,000 retained profit as a resilience buffer. That buffer matters now: absenteeism stands at 10%, the 6.1% minimum wage rise looms, and SCL will still need $600 per employee to finish solar-roof safety training for 14 staff without touching member funds.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to Suncourt Logistics and its solar array and van decision.

questions.question_text: SCL is launching its solar-powered, low-carbon delivery service for regional grocery retailers. Consider a full-page advert in the regional newspaper, a community open evening at the new solar-powered hub for retailer customers, or a trade exhibition stand at the national grocery logistics expo. Which should SCL choose to promote the launch? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
Regional newspaper advertising: A full-page advert would tell 8,400 retailers and shoppers in SCL's catchment about the two solar hubs, the 1.9 GWh generated last quarter and the 95.1% on-time rate on 18,400 last-mile deliveries. It is familiar, locally trusted and reasonably priced, but readership is broad — many are consumers, not buyers — response is slow to attribute to delivered contracts, and the message cannot be experienced the way a working solar hub can.

Open evening at the solar-powered hub: Inviting regional retailer customers to walk the roof, see live delivery vans load, meet the member-drivers and taste groceries delivered by a cooperative makes SCL's whole value proposition tangible in an evening. It converts the 62% of 700 surveyed customers wanting a renewable-energy cooperative supplier, lets the 49% willing to accept slower lower-carbon windows discuss terms face to face, and generates stories for local press at trivial cost; its reach is limited to invited guests, so conversion depends on a strong invite list.

National grocery logistics expo: An expo stand would put SCL in front of grocery procurement teams from beyond its two-hub catchment, build national credibility and rival listings opportunities; but exhibition fees, stand build and travel make it expensive for a regional co-op, most attendees will never use two distribution hubs, and fleet-national rivals outspend SCL on presence.

Recommendation: SCL should choose the community open evening at the solar-powered hub. It is the cheapest, most persuasive route to the exact regional grocery retailers who can sign with SCL tomorrow, it showcases assets no advert can fake, and it reinforces the cooperative and renewable identity its 62% preference score depends on. The newspaper is rejected as untargeted broadcast awareness, and the expo is rejected as over-budget and over-geography for a two-hub cooperative; SCL can layer modest local press coverage around the open evening for extra reach.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited knowledge or outline of the promotion options with minimal context.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed discussion of the advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of SCL with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of SCL with a well-justified recommendation explaining why newspaper advertising and the expo are rejected.

questions.question_text: SCL's absenteeism among warehouse operatives and drivers has reached 10%. Explain two benefits for SCL of using profit sharing to motivate its 85 staff.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Profit sharing ties every operative's and driver's reward directly to the surplus the cooperative distributes, so good attendance, careful loading and on-time drops all feed the same pot they share. For a cooperative facing 10% absenteeism, that alignment turns each shift into a shared financial interest — operatives cover for absent colleagues, drivers avoid no-shows, and the 95.1% on-time rate and falling complaint count (31 to 19 per month) translate into tangible year-end payments.

Point 2: Profit sharing suits SCL's cooperative culture better than piece-rate bonuses, reinforcing teamwork across the two hubs and toward the new third array rather than individual competition. It also costs nothing when the co-op has a poor year, protecting the $510,000 fixed-cost base during the 6.1% wage rise, and it signals that members genuinely prosper with the business — lifting retention, cutting the $600 per replacement forklift or solar-roof training spend, and protecting the 48,000 units a year delivered to regional grocery retailers.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SCL's absenteeism, cooperative culture and complaint rate.

questions.question_text: SCL must train 14 staff in forklift and solar-roof safety. Consider on-the-job training mentored by senior warehouse supervisors or off-the-job training at the regional skills centre. Which should SCL choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Mentoring by SCL's senior supervisors teaches exactly the forklift routes, racking heights and loading-dock routines in use today, costs nothing in fees, and keeps all 14 staff productive while covering for 10% absenteeism. Drawbacks are that supervisors lose picking and loading hours, poor habits pass between generations of operatives, and work at height on the solar roofs cannot be certified informally — a serious liability gap if an untrained operative ever walks the array after maintenance.

Off-the-job training: The regional skills centre course at $600 per employee gives all 14 staff assessed forklift and roof safety qualifications, costing $8,400 in total — trivial against $950,000 of planned expansion. Staff are removed from shifts for the course, however, tightening cover at peak delivery windows, and generic course content only partly matches SCL's racking layout, array mounting systems and two-hub traffic flows, so site-specific shadowing would still be needed afterwards.

Decision: SCL should choose off-the-job training at the regional skills centre for all 14 staff, paired with short on-site shadowing on return. Forklift and roof work combine high harm potential with legal and insurer expectations of recognised certification, and the $8,400 fee is noise next to the $950,000 investment in the third array; an at-height incident on an uncertified roof would close the hub far harder than two training days would. Pure on-the-job training is rejected as non-compliant for roof access, though on-site mentoring remains right for day-to-day forklift polish after certification.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to SCL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of one or both training methods in the context of SCL.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods in the context of SCL with a well-justified decision covering cost, safety, compliance and certification.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how SCL's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $510,000 ÷ ($46 − $30) = $510,000 ÷ $16 = 31,875 units. Answer: break-even output is 31,875 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $46 − $30 = $16.00. Answer: contribution per unit is $16.00.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways SCL's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. SCL's managers can compare the 31,875-unit break-even output with actual output of 48,000 units to confirm the cooperative is comfortably profitable, with a margin of safety of 16,125 units, informing whether the third solar array can support added delivery volume.
2. Contribution per unit of $16 lets SCL model discounts for volume retailer contracts, for example a cut to $43 would drop contribution to $13, letting managers judge whether slower lower-carbon windows for the 49% of flexible customers still cover the $510,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs of $510,000 and contribution per unit helps managers verify affordability of the $600,000 bank loan for the array and van fleet by checking annual surplus against scheduled instalments under both current and pessimistic volumes.
4. Managers can use average total cost of $40.63 ($510,000 ÷ 48,000 + $30) to benchmark the two electric hubs against any future grid-powered rival, track the solar saving as electricity prices rise 17.5%, and set productivity expectations of roughly 565 units per employee across the 85-strong workforce.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 31,875 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $16.00 | (iii) Four contextual uses explained: margin of safety of 16,125 units vs 48,000-unit output; retailer contract discount modelling vs $510,000 fixed costs; bank loan affordability check for the $600,000 agreement; and average total cost benchmarking at $40.63 to capture solar savings as electricity prices rise.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate SCL's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has SCL's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 35.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 40.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 10.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 14.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 21.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 revenue = $7,500,000 and gross profit = $2,625,000 against cost of sales of $4,875,000; 2025 revenue = $8,400,000 and gross profit = $3,360,000 against cost of sales of $5,040,000. 2024 operating profit = $750,000 against $7,500,000 of revenue (10.0%); 2025 operating profit = $1,176,000 against $8,400,000 of revenue (14.0%). 2024 capital employed = $5,000,000, 2025 = $5,600,000; interest payable rose from $210,000 to $246,000. 2024 figure: $750,000 ÷ $5,000,000 = 15.0% on capital employed; 2025 figure: $1,176,000 ÷ $5,600,000 = 21.0%.

Evaluation: SCL's profitability has strengthened markedly. Margins widened because revenue grew $900,000 while cost of sales grew only $165,000, evidence that solar coverage (71% of demand, up from 58%) and electric-van efficiency are cutting the cost of every delivery while cooperatives retain price loyalty. Operating profit jumped by $426,000, easily covering the $36,000 rise in interest payable. However, capital employed grew 12% from $5,000,000 to $5,600,000 and will rise again with the $950,000 expansion; the 6.1% wage increase and 10% absenteeism will test whether these margins survive contact with a full payroll. Rising grocery-contract volumes are essential to keep the new array's fixed savings compounding.

Conclusion: SCL's financial performance has improved. Gross profit margin rose from 35.0% to 40.0%, the operating profit margin rose from 10.0% to 14.0%, and ROCE rose from 15.0% to 21.0%. The cooperative should proceed with the third rooftop array and 40 electric vans, but must pair the investment with profit sharing and tighter attendance management to protect its new margins through the wage rise.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate ratio calculations for both years combined with detailed evaluation of revenue, cost of sales, operating profit and capital employed movements and a justified conclusion on whether SCL's financial performance improved.

questions.question_text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for SCL of introducing rooftop solar across its distribution hubs.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Rooftop solar already covers 71% of warehouse electricity demand, up from 58%, so the third array locks in permanent insulation against the 17.5% year-on-year rise in commercial electricity prices. It strengthens SCL's pitch to the 62% of 700 surveyed retailers who prefer a renewable-energy cooperative supplier, cuts the $30 variable cost per unit, and reinforces the low-carbon story that justifies SCL's $46 selling price against grid-powered competitors paying full tariffs.

Disadvantage: The $950,000 commitment — $600,000 bank loan plus $350,000 retained profit — concentrates capital in hardware whose winter output and shading losses can undershoot forecasts exactly when delivery demand peaks. Roof-mounted arrays also add maintenance, insurance and safety-training burdens at height, and any storm damage to the hub roof halts solar generation while repairs proceed — at which point the $510,000 fixed-cost base and delivery schedules could strain just as the 6.1% wage rise lands.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to SCL's solar data, costs and expansion.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the 17.5% rise in commercial electricity prices, the 6.1% minimum wage increase and the base interest rate rise to 5.25% will affect SCL. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Electricity price rise (17.5% year-on-year): For grid-powered rivals this is brutal, but for SCL it is close to a structural advantage: the rooftop arrays already cover 71% of warehouse demand, so the cooperative keeps buying only the residual 29% from the grid while competitors pay the full tariff. The saving per unit delivered grows with each quarter of solar output, reinforcing the renewable pricing story retailers value. The downside is narrower: maintenance and insurance on the arrays become more important as replacement parts also inflate, and the 29% residual still stings.

Minimum wage increase (6.1%, to $13.53 per hour): With 85 staff — warehouse operatives, drivers and office — payroll is SCL's largest cost. If average hourly pay is around $13.53, one full-time employee costs roughly $28,100 a year, so a 6.1% rise adds about $1,710 per worker, roughly $145,000 across the workforce. That is a direct hit on the operating profit figure that rose from $750,000 to $1,176,000, lands on top of 10% absenteeism cover costs, and risks squeezing member surplus distributions in the year the third array is commissioned.

Interest rate rise (4.5% to 5.25%): Only the $600,000 bank loan is affected, adding about $4,500 a year of interest — manageable against the $246,000 interest figure already booked, and partly avoidable by fixing the loan or by member decision at the annual AGM. It is the smallest of the three changes in cash terms, though it makes any future fleet expansion borrowing costlier.

Conclusion: The 6.1% minimum wage increase will have the greatest impact. It is the largest unavoidable cash exposure at roughly $145,000 a year, it compounds with absenteeism and recruitment cover, and it lands directly on the $1,176,000 operating profit through the payroll that underpins all 48,000 units a year. The electricity rise actually flatters SCL's solar investment by widening the gap with grid-powered rivals, and the interest move is trivial at $4,500 a year; SCL should respond with tighter rostering, profit sharing, and surplus distribution planning rather than price increases.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to SCL.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on SCL's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three external changes in the context of SCL with a well-justified judgement that the minimum wage increase has the greatest impact and why the other two are smaller or favourable.
